thread.title: Broadcom: This Fast Growing, 4.6% Yielding Blue-Chip Is The Best Tech Stock You Can Buy Today - Broadcom Limited (NASDAQ:AVGO)

author: Dividend Sensei
title: Broadcom: This Fast Growing, 4.6% Yielding Blue-Chip Is The Best Tech Stock You Can Buy Today - Broadcom Limited (NASDAQ:AVGO)
text:
(Source: imgflip )
My goal is to help readers achieve their long-term financial dreams, and historically speaking, dividend growth stocks have been the best performing asset class you can own.
Not just do they tend to deliver superior total returns over time, but they also do so with less volatility, which lets you sleep better at night during inevitable market corrections like we're experiencing now.
Well, when it comes to tech blue-chips, few stocks can match Broadcom's ( AVGO ) impressive track record of 57.5% CAGR payout growth over the past eight years.
AVGO Dividend data by YCharts
Not surprisingly that epic dividend growth has caused Broadcom to outperform both the S&P 500 and most other tech stocks as well.
AVGO Total Return Price data by YCharts
And with the company just announcing a 51% dividend hike , this means that Broadcom is now trading at its highest yield ever (4.6%) making it a sensational high-yield income growth investment.
In fact, there are four reasons why I consider Broadcom to be the best high-yield tech blue-chip you can buy today. That includes not just great management and a fantastic long-term growth runway, but thanks to the recent correction in tech in general, and semiconductor stocks in particular, Broadcom is currently between 24% and 35% undervalued. That means that investors who buy today can not only lock in generous, safe and fast-growing income but likely 18% to 21% long-term annualized total returns.
1. Broadcom's Cash-Rich Business Model Continues To Deliver Strong Growth Where It Matters Most Broadcom was founded in the 1960s and has a rich history of pioneering technology like LED displays and fiber optic transmitters and receivers. As a result of its decades of heavy but focused R&D spending, Broadcom has over 23,000 patents with about another 2,000 pending.
(Source: investor presentation )
Over the decades Broadcom has built itself into a global leader in: data center networking, home connectivity, broadband access, telecommunications equipment, smartphones, base stations, data center servers and storage, factory automation, power generation, alternative energy systems, and electronic displays.
That's been through a large number of well-executed strategic mergers and acquisitions, the largest which was $37 billion merger with Avago technologies in 2016. The reason for that acquisition was Avago's dominance in radio frequency or RF filters for smartphones (about 30% of sales) including in the Apple ( AAPL ) iPhone and Samsung Galaxy phone lines. That was added to Broadcom's legacy strengths, which are in networking switches, Wi-Fi chips, set-top box chips, enterprise storage chips, mainframe software, and fiber channel switch products. All told the company's numerous purchases have created one the most diversified chip makers in the world.
Wired infrastructure: 41% of Q4 revenue (3% YOY growth) Wireless communications: 31% of Q4 revenue (-5% YOY growth) Enterprise storage: 23% of Q4 revenue (96% YOY growth due to Brocade acquisition) Industrial: 5% of Q4 revenue (6% YOY growth) Broadcom's strategy for M&A is to buy top #1 or #2 industry leaders but at reasonable or even cheap valuations. It then integrates the most profitable and fastest growing segments, achieves good cost synergies, and sells off commoditized and lower profitable businesses.
Combined with its leading economies of scale and strong patent portfolio this creates an incredibly profitable business model. One that in fiscal 2018 generated sensational 39.5% free cash flow margins. Free cash flow is what's left over after running the company and investing in future growth (including capex and R&D). It's what pays for dividends, buybacks and repays debt.
Company Gross Margin Operating Margin Net Margin FCF Margin Broadcom 53.9% 26.8% 23.6% 39.5% Industry Average 27.5% 6.8% 5.3% NA (Sources: earnings release, Gurufocus)
Not just is Broadcom one of the most profitable semiconductor makers today, but it's also growing at an impressive rate.
Metric Fiscal 2018 Revenue Growth 18% Adjusted EPS Growth 30% Free Cash Flow Growth 50% Dividend Growth 51% (Source: earnings release)
That includes both in its top and bottom line, including 30% growth in adjusted EPS but most importantly 50% growth in free cash flow. That's what allowed management to recently hike the dividend by 51% for 2019.
(Source: investor presentation)
And lest you think that 2018 was merely a fluke, rest assured that Broadcom has a great track record of maintaining industry-leading growth rates as well as steadily improving profitability. That's especially impressive for a cyclical industry such as this and has largely been made possible by a steady stream of well thought out and executed acquisitions. For example, the $18.9 billion acquisition of CA Technologies closed on November 5th, one day after the fiscal fourth quarter ended. That acquisition is expected to drive continued strong growth next year, in both the top and bottom line.
2019 Revenue Growth: 18% 2019 Adjusted EPS growth: 13.6% 2019's strong results are not just due to the CA tech acquisition closing. According to CEO Hock Tan "our outlook for the semiconductor business is for modest revenue growth in 2019." That might not sound like much but keep in mind that many chip makers are expecting flat or even negative top-line growth next year. And management had an important announcement at its last conference call regarding a change in CA Tech's business model as well.
" We expect these changes to result in a dramatically more profitable revenue base which is more aligned to the rest of Broadcom and that we expect will grow. First and foremost, gone are the days of trying to land new products with new customers and I am referring to software, enterprise software. We are focusing all our attention on renewing existing products with existing mainframe-centric customers, customers that represent virtually all of the world’s largest enterprises and largest spenders on IT. We are also targeting expansion opportunities within this core mainframe customer base. The cost of running this renewed and expanded model will be substantially less than the legacy land-at-all-cost model and importantly renewing and expanding plays to CA’s strengths. " Hock Tan (emphasis added)
The reason I bring this up is that Broadcom has a great track record of FCF conversion (FCF/EPS). With the company shifting towards a leaner operating model at CA Tech this likely means that next year's FCF/share growth will come in above the 13.6% Adjusted EPS growth expected from management's 2019 guidance. In fact, as I'll soon explain management is hinting that FCF/share could rise as much as 20% in fiscal 2019.
And by 2020 Broadcom expects its adjusted operating margins to increase from 51% in 2019 to 55% thanks largely to CA Tech's focus on "an all-you-can-eat subscription-based model" that is expected to reduce annual operating costs by $1.5 billion to $1.6 billion per year.
2. Long-Term Growth Dividend Potential Remains Excellent Thanks To Proven Shareholder Friendly Management Team And Clear Growth Runway The key to good long-term investments is the quality of the management team, but also the corporate culture. You want not just a proven skilled team of capital allocators working to grow your business, but also one that will reward you with handsome dividend growth over time.
Broadcom is led by CEO Hock Tan who has was Avago's chief executive since 2006. What's especially notable about Mr. Tan is that he has a strong background in both engineering and finance. For example, he has a master's in mechanical engineering but has also served in financial roles at Pepsi ( PEP ), General Motors ( GM ), as well as at several hedge funds.
This explains why Avago under Tan was able to pull off such strong deals including the following acquisitions.
CyOptics: $400 million in 2013 LSI Corp.: $6.6 billion in 2014 PLX Tech: $300 million in 2014 Emulex: $606 million in 2015 Broadcom/Avago Tech merger: $37 billion in 2016 Brocade: $6 billion in 2017 CA Technologies: $18.9 billion in 2018 According to the Harvard Business Review, 70% to 90% of mergers fail, due to incompatible corporate cultures/supply chains, and failed synergies. Mr. Tan has managed to do what very few CEOs have done, which is consistently make sound M&A deals that result in excellent long-term growth in cash flow, dividends, and shareholder value.
This skilled management team is benefiting from a clear and large growth runway, that's continuing to grow larger thanks to its acquisitions (more than tripled in recent years). One of the best growth catalysts for Broadcom is in digital cloud computing (its enterprise storage business). Even stripping out the Brocade acquisition revenue growth in that business segment was double-digits in the last quarter.
(Source: Gartner)
According to the analyst firm Gartner, between 2016 and 2020 the cloud computing market is going to nearly double . That's to support not just the rise of corporate IT's transition to cloud computing but also the ongoing explosion of data created by the world's ongoing shift to mobile data consumption as well as the internet of things or IOT.
(Source: Cisco Systems)
Combined with the coming shift to 5G telecom, the internet of things will allow for the connection of hundreds of billions of devices to the internet ( 200 billion devices by 2020 ), ushering in a future of driverless cars, AI-driven deep data analysis, and increasing factory automation (just 10% of the world's factories are currently automated). These are all markets that Broadcom has been focusing on with a steady increase in R&D to deliver industry-leading solutions to customers.
(Source: investor presentation)
AVGO Research and Development Expense (TTM) data by YCharts
Broadcom estimates that its total addressable market will soon surpass $200 billion, which when combined with its strong position in chips to serve all these markets should allow for long-term revenue growth of about 5%. Through buybacks and improving economies of scale (higher operating margins), the company expects that to translate into long-term double-digit growth in earnings and free cash flow per share.
(Source: Broadcom CA Tech acquisition fact sheet )
More importantly, the CA Technologies acquisitions mean that about 20% of its revenue will now be in the form of recurring software-based revenue.
(Source: investor presentation)
That kind of stable and recurring revenue is going to help Broadcom remain one of the most shareholder-friendly chip makers in terms of capital returns to investors.
(Source: investor presentation)
The company's goal is to pay out 50% of FCF as dividends, and use the remaining half to buyback shares and help fund future acquisitions.
For fiscal 2019 that translates to about $12 billion in buybacks and dividends, according to CFO Tom Krause.
"Consistent with our capital allocation policy, we will reassess the dividend at this time next year based on our fiscal 2019 free cash flow from operations... we are also budgeting to return an additional $8 billion to stockholders through stock buybacks in fiscal 2019 . Coupled with the dividend, this means we are planning to return approximately $12 billion to stockholders in fiscal 2019 , which constitutes all of our projected free cash flow, plus the excess cash that we have on our balance sheet today." - CFO Tom Krause (emphasis added)
Even more exciting? According to management its strong growth in 2019, combined with fast-rising margins due to the new CA Tech business model, means that Broadcom investors might see a 20% dividend hike next year and double-digit long-term payout growth.
"So when you do that math, you are going to come up with a number that’s north of 20% in terms of potential for dividend growth (for 2019). Now, going forward we will have a couple of other tailwinds that we have benefited from in the past, which is frankly M&A and the accretion that we drive once we are fully integrated and restructured. And so as Hock has been articulating, when we get to the $2.5 billion-plus of operating profit, that’s going to start to be realized in 2020, into 2021. Absent additional M&A, we would continue to focus not just on the dividend but also the buyback, which would allow us to reduce the share count as well. So I think we have a good setup to continue to be able to drive the dividend well into the double digits over the next several years. " - CFO Tom Krause
The bottom line is that Broadcom offers not just a great chip business, but now has a strong foothold in recurring software revenue as well. That in turn likely means that income investors can enjoy not just a generous, safe and fast-growing dividend for the foreseeable future, but most likely market-crushing total returns as well.
3. Dividend Profile: Generous, Safe, And Fast Growing Dividend Plus Market Crushing Return Potential The most important part of any income investment is the dividend profile which consists of three parts: yield, safety, and long-term growth potential. Combined with valuation this is what tends to drive total returns over time.
Company Yield FCF Payout Ratio Simply Safe Dividend Safety Score (Out Of 100) Projected 10 Year Dividend Growth (Analyst Consensus) 10 Year Potential Annual Total Return (No Valuation Change) Valuation Adjusted 10 Year Return Potential
Broadcom 4.6% 58% (2018) 46% (2019) 87 (Very Safe) 12% to 13% 15.6% to 16.6% 19.9% to 20.9% S&P 500 2.0% 38% NA 6.4% 8.40% 0% to 5% (Sources: management guidance, Gurufocus, Fast Graphs, Simply Safe Dividends, Morningstar, BlackRock, Vanguard, Gordon Dividend Growth Model, Dividend Yield Theory, Multipl.com, Yardeni Research, moneychimp)
Thanks to its massive 51% dividend hike Broadcom's yield is among the highest in the tech industry or any US company for that matter. More importantly, that dividend represents a safe 58% payout ratio from fiscal 2018's free cash flow and less than 50% of 2019's expected FCF.
The other half of the dividend safety equation is the balance sheet.
Company Debt/EBITDA Interest Coverage Ratio Debt/Capital Current Ratio S&P Credit Rating Average Interest Cost
Broadcom 2.0 14.5 42% 4.0 BBB- 3.4% Industry Average 1.7 57.8 44% 2.2 NA NA (Sources: Morningstar, Gurufocus, CSImarketing, Fastgraphs)
It's true that Broadcom's M&A happy strategy has meant above average debt levels. However, note that Broadcom's massive river of cash flow, which is becoming increasingly stable over time (due to software sales) is still easily covering its interest costs. And on a debt/capital and current ratio (short-term assets/short-term liabilities) basis, the company's dividend doesn't appear to be at risk from its debt, 99% of which is fixed-rate. That's why Broadcom still has an investment grade balance sheet, which management expects to maintain going forward. That allows it to borrow at low-interest rates which are nearly four times lower than its returns on invested capital.
Since 1956 the Gordon Dividend Growth Model or GDGM has proven relatively effective at predicting total returns. This formula says that over time total returns = yield + long-term cash flow/dividend growth. That's because a stock's price is a function of its cash flow and assuming a constant payout ratio (which Broadcom plans to now maintain) the share price should track the dividend over time. The current yield and long-term growth expectations of 12.8% (10-year analyst consensus growth forecast) mean that Broadcom should be able to deliver an exceptional 17.4% CAGR long-term total return over the next decade. That's assuming no changes to its valuation.
For context, the S&P 500's historical total return is 9.2% , and the GDGM is expecting just 8.4% CAGR total returns from the market over the coming years. Morningstar, BlackRock, and Vanguard are even more bearish assuming the market will deliver just 0% to 5% total returns over the coming five to 10 years from today's valuation.
Thus Broadcom is currently offering:
more than double the market's yield about double the S&P 500's historical dividend growth rate (6.4% since 1990) far superior total return potential And when we consider Broadcom's valuation adjusted return potential than the case for buying the stock today gets even stronger.
Valuation: A World Class Company At A Fantastic Price AVGO Total Return Price data by YCharts
Broadcom has had a rough year, thanks to general weakness in chip makers, concerns over its CA Tech acquisition (software company acquisitions are a new strategy), and of course two market corrections. But that just means that AVGO is one of the most undervalued high-yield tech blue-chips you can buy today.
As a semiconductor maker (a cyclical industry) Broadcom's historical forward PE ratio has never been that high. However, today the stock is trading at a single-digit earnings multiple that is pricing in nearly zero long-term growth.
Forward PE 5-year average Forward PE Long-term Growth Rate Baked Into Price Analyst 10-Year Growth Consensus
9.9 12.8 0.7% 12.8% (Sources: Simply Safe Dividends, Benjamin Graham, Fast Graphs)
Remember that management expects to deliver double-digit earnings growth over the coming years, and analysts think the actual growth rate will be nearly 13%. This implies that Broadcom is set for major multiple expansion that would boost its total returns far above what's predicted by the GDGM (which assumes a stock starts and ends at fair value). What kind of valuation boost?
For that, I turn to my favorite dividend stock valuation method, dividend yield theory or DYT. This has proven highly effective since 1966 when asset manager/newsletter publisher Investment Quality Trends began exclusively using this valuation method to deliver decades of market-beating total returns.
(Source: Investment Quality Trends)
DYT merely says that since dividends are paid out of cash flow, which is what a stock's long-term price is based on, the yield (a proxy for P/FCF) should cycle around a relatively fixed point over time approximating fair value.
Yield 5 Year Average Yield 13 Year Median Yield Estimated Fair Value Yield Discount To Fair Value
4.6% 3.0% 1.3% 3.0% 35% (Sources: Simply Safe Dividends, Gurufocus, Dividend Yield Theory)
Now in the case of Broadcom, we need to use its five-year average yield since the company only became a dividend growth stock in 2010. Over the past five year's AVGO's average yield was 3.0%. That implies that the stock is about 35% undervalued, and would have to rise 53% to return its yield to its historical norm.
Estimated Fair Value Upside To Fair Value Long-Term (10 Year) Valuation Boost Valuation Adjusted Total Return Potential
$353 53% 4.3% CAGR 19.9% to 20.9% (Sources: Dividend Yield Theory, moneychimp, Gordon Dividend Growth Model, Fast Graphs)
I can't predict how quickly Broadcom's yield mean reverts but over a 10-year time frame, it's a near certainty. That would translate into shares outpacing FCF and dividends by 4.3% CAGR over the next decade and delivering 20% to 21% long-term total returns. That's a roughly 700% total return expectation which is slightly less than what the company has delivered over the past eight years.
One other valuation approach I sometimes like to use for large-cap blue-chips is Morningstar's three-stage discounted cash flow or DCF model. Morningstar analysts are famous for their long-term fundamental approach and conservative growth assumptions.
Morningstar Fair Value Discount To Fair Value Long-Term Valuation Boost Total Return Potential
$300 24% 2.8% 18.4% to 19.4% (Sources: Morningstar, Fast Graphs, Moneychimp, Gordon Dividend Growth Model)
Morningstar currently estimates Broadcom's intrinsic value at $300 implying a 24% margin of safety and a 2.8% long-term valuation boost. That still translates into about 19% expected long-term total returns.
For a company of Broadcom's quality, I'm more than happy to recommend buying at fair value. So when I see this fast growing tech blue-chip trading for a 24% to 35% discount, and sporting its highest yield ever, I'm eager to pound the table with a "very strong buy" recommendation.
In fact, as far as high-yield tech blue-chips go Broadcom is my strongest recommendation right now, at least for anyone comfortable with its risk profile.
Risks To Keep In Mind While I consider Broadcom a low-risk blue-chip (from a dividend safety perspective) there are nonetheless several risks to keep in mind. The first is that while Tan has a great M&A track record, even he doesn't bat 1.000. For example, President Trump blocked the company's attempted $121 billion acquisition of Qualcomm ( QCOM ). While that deal made a great deal of financial sense for Broadcom, it shows that the companies M&A heavy growth strategy might not be able to continue delivering the kinds of strong growth investors have come to expect over the last few years.
We also can't forget that Broadcom's core business, semiconductors, is inherently cyclical, especially since the RF smartphone business has relatively high customer concentration with Apple (about 20%) and Foxconn (11%). The company's top five customers accounted for 42% of revenue in the first three quarters of fiscal 2018. While Broadcom's ability to continue finding attractive acquisition targets has allowed it to deliver industry-leading growth in a cyclical business that might now always be the case, especially during a global recession.
(Source: Broadcom 10K)
Next, we have to remember that Broadcom has a lot of currency risk since it pays dividends in US dollars but 87% of fiscal year's 2017 revenues were from overseas. Note that Chinese sales have typically accounted for over 50% of revenue, due to Broadcom's major clients being OEMs and contract manufacturers located in that country. This means that should the US/China trade negotiations fail, and 25% tariffs are imposed on all Chinese imports, then Broadcom could face a steep hit to its top and bottom lines. Of course, if we get a trade deal (which I consider likely by February 2019) then Broadcom is likely a coiled spring set to soar.
Finally, we can't forget that while Broadcom's dividend growth track record is impressive, in the future investors can't expect anywhere close to the magnitude of dividend hikes that they've enjoyed in the past. That dividend growth was largely a function of FCF payout ratio expansion which management says is now over. Over the long-term, adjusting for the cyclical nature of its industry, Broadcom expects to deliver double-digit earnings and free cash flow growth, which will mean dividend growth along the same lines. But in future investors might even see a year or two of frozen dividends if the chip industry experiences an especially bad downturn.
Bottom Line: Broadcom Is The Best High-Yield Tech Blue-Chip You Can Buy Today There's nothing better than buying a quality high-yield blue chip during a market downturn. Today Broadcom, with its mouthwatering safe yield, fast long-term growth outlook, and proven industry-leading management team, is one of the best long-term income investments you can make and my strongest tech recommendation at this time.
That's courtesy of not just the massive long-term growth runway the company faces, but the highly shareholder-friendly corporate culture as well. One that believes in smart capital allocation in terms of both R&D and M&A, but also in returning all free cash flow to shareholders.
With Broadcom now 24% to 35% undervalued, it's a fantastic time to add this proven winner to your diversified portfolio. That will allow you to not just lock in a generous, safe and fast-growing dividend, but also likely 18% to 21% long-term total returns as well.
